title-group.article-title: Growth performance and antioxidant response of broiler chicken fed oxidized lipids with or without phytogenic feed additives

abstract.p: The aim of this study was to test the in vivo antioxidant capacity in broilers of two phytogenic additives, one derived from olive pomace (OE) and an encapsulated product based on Capsicum sp., black pepper, and ginger (SPICY), in a challenge using oxidized lipids in the feed. A total of 720 one-day-old male Cobb 500 were allocated to 72 pens (8 treatments, 9 replicates, 10 birds/replicate). The treatments were arranged in a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, the factors being: fat source (4% soybean oil or 4% peroxidized soybean oil); SPICY (0 or 250 ppm); and OE (0 or 3077 ppm). From 1 to 21 days (global period) no significant differences were observed on performance. Broilers fed peroxidized oil showed higher plasma ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP; P < 0.05) values and higher catalase (CAT) activity compared to those fed fresh oil except in those birds fed the OE which remained constant with both oil sources (P < 0.05 for the interaction). Broilers fed OE showed a significant lower CAT gene expression in the liver (P < 0.05). Moreover, the heat shock protein 70 (HSP70) gene expression was lower in birds fed fresh oil and OE compared to those fed fresh oil without OE but higher in birds fed peroxidized oil and OE compared to those fed peroxidized oil without OE (P < 0.05 for the interaction). By contrast, broilers fed SPICY upregulated CAT (P < 0.05) and downregulated HSP70 (P < 0.05) gene expression in the liver compared to those not supplemented with SPICY. In conclusion, feeding broilers with peroxidized soybean oil from 1 to 21 days of age did not affect the productive parameters. However, the presence of lipid peroxidation products in the feed triggered both non-enzymatic and enzymatic antioxidant responses to maintain the oxidant/antioxidant balance. In the case of birds fed the OE, the enzymatic antioxidant response was more attenuated, indicating a better control of oxidative stress, likely mediated by HSP70.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: During the past years plant-derived feed additives have gained increasing interest for promoting animal health and growth (Zeng et al., 2015; Varricchio, et al., 2019). The growth-promoting effects of plant-derived feed additives are generally attributed to their antimicrobial, antioxidant, and immune modulatory effects (Zeng et al., 2015). While most research has focused on including phytogenic feed additives into strategies aimed at replacing antibiotics as growth promoters, less attention has been given to their role in enhancing animal antioxidant defenses against oxidative stress (Mountzouris et al., 2020).

Oxidative stress in poultry production can arise from various common stressors, both external (e.g., temperature, light, feed) and internal (e.g., toxins, pathogens), which may also interact with each other (Balakrishnan et al., 2023). These stressors negatively impact the antioxidant status of the broilers, unbalancing the endogenous antioxidant response and the free radical production, leading to lipid peroxidation, protein and DNA damage and apoptosis (Basiouni et al., 2023). Stress triggers the defence mechanisms of the body, leading to a higher demand for energy, amino acids, vitamins, and minerals which might have a negative impact in the animal performance (Surai, 2015). Furthermore, fat-soluble vitamins that are crucial to the antioxidant response, such vitamin E, may get oxidised and lose their antioxidant activity due to excessive lipid peroxidation (Tesoriere et al., 1997; Ravisankar et al., 2015; Bacou et al., 2021).

In commercial broiler diets, vegetable oils and animal fats are utilized to increase the energy density of the feed and to enhance the growth rate and feed efficiency of broilers (Zhang et al., 2011). Among the available oil sources for broiler feed, vegetable oils are particularly rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and are highly digestible for broilers. However, PUFAs are also highly susceptible to oxidation during manufacturing or storage, generating undesirable compounds such as peroxides, aldehydes, ketones, and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 2015). These compounds can trigger oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, potentially harming gut health, immunity, growth and development. Therefore, oxidized fats in feed, besides being a problem for chickens in practice, can be a valuable model for studying oxidative stress and evaluating the efficacy of feed antioxidants.

Because of their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties there is a growing interest in using plant-based additives in broiler diets to counteract oxidative stress coming from different productive factors including oxidized fats (Basiouni et al., 2023). In a previous dose‑response study, Corrales et al. (2023) found that partially replacing vitamin E with an olive pomace extract produced positive effects on FCR during the starter phase (1–7 days), with optimal results when the extract provided 22.5 mg/kg of hydroxytyrosol (HT). Also, Herrero-Encinas et al. (2023) using 250 ppm of a capsaicin-based additive (plus black pepper and ginger) and Sevillano et al. (2025) using similar quantities of these two additives, showed that these phytogenic additives could maintain or improve performance in low vitamin E diets through different antioxidant mechanisms of action, especially during the starter phase. Other studies like those carried out by Dias et al. (2023) found improvements in the fatty acid profile and a reduction in lipid peroxidation of the meat, bind to improvements of the anti-inflammatory response of broilers using 50 ppm of HT. Also, Li et al. (2022) found better performance, meat quality, immune response and better digestive enzyme secretion in broilers fed with a capsaicin-based additive with inclusion levels between 2 and 6 ppm. Phytogenic compounds such as polyphenols might support avian redox homeostasis by directly neutralizing free radicals and by inducing antioxidant enzyme activity through Nrf2 activation (Basiouni et al., 2023). Moreover, they can positively affect the oxidative processes of vitamin E and, thus, influence its recycling (Reboul, 2019). This may be of particular interest in young birds, in which their vitamin E recycling system does not seem to be as effective as in adult birds, and whose vitamin E levels decline rapidly during the first 14 days of life (Leeson, 2007; Surai et al., 2019). Chicks experience significant oxidative stress immediately after hatching, highlighting a substantial need for antioxidant protection during this early developmental stage that is mainly covered by vitamin E stores (Coudert et al., 2023).

With the aim to strengthen the antioxidant system of chickens during the first weeks of life, the present study explores the potential use of two phytogenic additives, an olive pomace and a spice-based extracts, as antioxidants in broiler starter feeds. To this end, the effects of the two phytogenic additives alone or in combination were tested in broiler chickens fed diets containing either fresh or oxidized fats for 21 days. Our study hypothesizes that the complementary mechanisms and potential synergistic interactions between water‑soluble antioxidants (e.g., polyphenols) and lipid‑soluble antioxidants (e.g., vitamin E) might enhance the antioxidant defence system of chicks during the first weeks of age.

sec.title: Material and methods
sec.p: The procedures used in this research were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (Permission No. 2021-001) and followed the Spanish Guidelines for the Care and Use of Animals in Research (Boletín Oficial del Estado, 2013).

sec.title: Birds and Husbandry
sec.p: The research was conducted at the experimental facilities of the Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (Department of Agricultural Production, ETSIAAB). A total of 720 one-day-old male broiler chicks (Cobb 500, 41.6 ± 0.83 g) were randomly allotted to 72 floor pens (0.96×1.5 m) in groups of 10, distributed across two similar rooms (36 pens per room). The pens were bedded with cereal straw pellets and equipped with 4 nipple drinkers and a hopper feeder. During the first week of age, additional first-age feeders were used. Water and feed were provided for ad libitum consumption throughout the experiment. The environmental conditions were automatically controlled according to commercial recommendations (Cobb Broiler, 2022). The temperature of the rooms was set at 33°C during the first week of age and then gradually reduced by 2°C per week until reaching 21°C at the end of the experiment. Birds received a light program of 23L:1D during the first week of age, which was progressively reduced to 18L:6D, keeping it until the end of the trial.

sec.title: Experimental design and diets
sec.p:
The experiment followed a randomized complete block design, with the room as a block. The 8 experimental diets were distributed across 72 pens, 36 in each room, resulting in 9 replicates per treatment. The experimental design was a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial arrangement, evaluating: 2 oil sources (4% of fresh soybean oil or 4% of peroxidized soybean oil), 2 levels of olive pomace extract (0 or 3077 ppm, providing 20 ppm of hydroxytyrosol, OE) and 2 levels of the spice extract (0 or 250 ppm, SPICY). The basal diet consisted of corn and soybean meal and were formulated to meet FEDNA (2018) nutrient requirements. Feeds were manufactured at the Instituto de Ciencia y Tecnología Animal of the Universitat Politècnica de València (Spain) in crumbles. Birds disposed feed and water ad libitum from days 1 to 21. Soybean oil peroxidation was induced by increasing the temperature to 95°C while bubbling air at a rate of 80L/min for 72 hours, following the conditions published by Lu et al. (2014). Phytogenic additives were added on top on the feeds and supplied by Lucta S.A. (Madrid, Spain). The OE consisted of a liquid fraction obtained from the olive pomace “alperujo” with a high concentration of polyphenols (more than 30 mEq of gallic acid per kg of product containing more than 1% of hydroxytyrosol). The SPICY additive was a fat-encapsulated extract composed of a blend of oleoresins from Capsicum sp., black pepper, and ginger, with capsaicin as the main active compound. sec.title: Laboratory feed analysis
sec.p:
Representative diet samples were ground using a laboratory mill (Retsch Model Z-I, Stuttgart, Germany) fitted with a 0.75 mm screen and analyzed for proximate composition. Moisture content was determined by oven-drying (method 930.15), ash by a muffle furnace incineration (method 942.05), and nitrogen by combustion (method 968.06) using a Leco equipment (FP-528, Leco Corporation, St. Joseph, MI) as indicated by AOAC International (2005) guidelines. Gross energy of the feed was measured using an adiabatic bomb calorimeter (model 6400, Parr Instrument Company, Moline, IL). Ether extract content was determined with an ANKOM XT10 extractor (ANKOM technology, NY, USA) as indicated in AOAC method 920.39. Vitamin E concentrations (α-tocopherol and γ-tocopherol) in the feed were quantified by HPLC according to official method (Directive 2000/45/EC). Hexanal concentration was determined using gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) coupled with solid-phase microextraction (SPME) of volatile compounds. Volatile compounds were analyzed using a 7890B gas chromatograph coupled to a 5977B mass detector (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), equipped with an HP-5 Ultra Inert column (30 m × 0.25 mm i.d. × 0.25 µm; Agilent Technologies). Hexanal quantification was performed using the standard addition method and processed with MassHunter software (Agilent Technologies). Peroxide value (PV) of feed was determined by the official method AOCS Cd-8b 90 (AOCS, 2009). Table 2 shows the analyzed composition of the 8 experimental diets.Table 2

sec.title: Animal performance and sampling
sec.p: Body weight and feed intake were measured at 10 and 21 days of age, and average daily gain, average daily feed intake and feed conversion ratio were calculated. Mortality was recorded as occurred. On day 21, one bird per pen was euthanized using a CO2 chamber. Samples of the right lobe of the liver were collected, frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80°C for oxidative stress-related gene expression analysis. Blood samples were also taken for the analysis of plasma antioxidant enzymes activity and non-enzymatic oxidative markers.

sec.title: Plasma analysis
sec.p: Plasma activity of three antioxidant enzymes was analyzed using commercial kits, following the instructions provided by the manufacturers: catalase (CAT; Cayman Chemical Kit catalogue no. 707002), Superoxide Dismutase (SOD; Cayman Chemical Kit catalogue no. 706002) and glutathione peroxidase (GPx; Cayman Chemical Kit catalogue no. 703102; Cayman Chemical, Ann Arbor, MI, USA). The content of vitamin E (α-tocopherol) in plasma was measured by HPLC following the method described by Rey et al. (2006). The free radical scavenging capacity of plasma was measured using the DPPH method (1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl) based on the reduction of the DPPH radical to the purple DPPH form, as described by Cecchini y Fazio (2020). The ferric reducing antioxidant power of plasma (FRAP), based on the reduction reaction between [Fe 3+ -(TPTZ) 2]3+ (tripyridyl triazine-ferric complex) and plasma antioxidants, giving Fe II and an intense blue color, was done following the procedure described by Benzie and Strain (1996). Thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) in plasma were measured modifying the spectrophotometric method described by Buege and Aust (1978). Perchloric acid was added to precipitate proteins. The protein-free supernatant was collected and mixed in a 1:2 proportion with thiobarbituric acid. The mixture was centrifuged for 10 minutes, and the absorbance was read at 532 nm using an UV-Vis spectrophotometer (ThermoFisher SkyHigh, ThermoFisher Scientific, Alcobendas, Spain). A standard curve was built with 1,1,3,3 tetraethoxypropane as standard in water perchloric acid.

sec.title: Gene expression analysis
sec.p:
Total RNA was extracted from 25 mg of liver tissue using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and a mixer mill MM-400 (Retsch, Stuttgart, Germany). RNA was isolated and purified using the PureLink RNA mini kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Massachusetts, USA). To avoid DNA contamination, a DNAse step was added to the “in column” procedure (RNAse-Free DNase Set, Quiagen, Australia). The extracted RNA was analyzed by spectrophotometry at 260/280 nm wavelengths (Epoch, BioTek, Winoosky, USA) using the Take3 Micro-Volume Plate (BioTek, Santa Barbara, USA), in order to determine their yield and quality. Once RNA was collected, a reverse transcription was done, mixing 2400 ng of the extracted RNA with the SuperScript VILO Master Mix (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, USA). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was done with a QuantStudioTM 5 Real-Time PCR Instrument (384-Well Block) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Carlsbad, CA, USA), using 10 μL of total reaction volume with PowerTrackTM SYBRTM Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Two housekeeping genes (β-Actin and Hypoxanthine Phosboribosyl-transferase) were used to normalize the expression of target genes (Table 3). Samples were analyzed in triplicate, with a non-template control as the negative control based on RNA/DNA free water. The efficiency of each qRT-RNA reaction was assessed by generating standard curves using cDNA.Table 3

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data were analyzed using the general linear model GLM procedure of SAS software (9.2, SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA), with the 3 main factors (fat source, OE and SPICY inclusion) and their interactions as fixed effects. The room was incorporated in the model as a block effect and initial BW was considered as a covariate. In case of gene expression data, for genes displaying efficiencies different from 2 (E ≠ 2), cycle threshold (Ct) values were adjusted according to the model described by Steibel et al. (2009). The standard error was used to recalculate the lower and upper 95% confidence intervals for each fold change.

sec.title: Growth performance
sec.p:
The growth performance results are shown in Table 4. At 10 days of age, birds fed OE had significantly lower BW, ADG and ADFI (P < 0.05). An interaction between the oil source and the SPICY inclusion was found for FCR (P < 0.05). Birds fed fresh oil and SPICY had a higher FCR compared to those fed oxidized oil and SPICY. There were no statistical differences between dietary treatments from 11 to 21 days of age, nor in the overall period. The global mortality rate was 1.81% with no differences between treatments.Table 4

sec.title: Antioxidant status and oxidative stress biomarkers in plasma
sec.p:
Broilers fed peroxidized oil showed higher FRAP values compared to those fed fresh oil (P < 0.05) (Table 5). Also, birds fed peroxidized oil tended to have higher DPPH values compared to those fed fresh oil (P = 0.077). No statistical differences or interactions were found between the main factors for TBARS values. Vitamin E in plasma, measured as α- and γ-tocopherol, was significantly lower in birds fed peroxidized oil compared to those birds fed fresh oil (P < 0.001). Birds fed peroxidized oil showed higher catalase (CAT) activity compared to those fed fresh oil except in those birds fed the OE which remained constant with both oil sources (P < 0.05 for the interaction; Fig. 1). A similar trend (P = 0.079) was found in GPx activity. No statistical differences were found in SOD activity between main factors.Table 5

sec.title: Gene expression
sec.p:
Results of gene expression in the liver are shown in Table 6. Broilers fed peroxidized oil significantly downregulated (P < 0.05) the liver expression of TTPA compared to those fed the fresh oil. Broilers fed SPICY supplemented diets showed a significant upregulation (P < 0.05) of liver CAT expression compared to those not supplemented with SPICY. By contrast, birds fed OE significantly downregulated liver CAT expression (P < 0.05) compared to those without OE. Broilers not receiving the SPICY additive showed a significant upregulation of liver HSP70 expression (P < 0.05) compared to those fed SPICY. Furthermore, a significant interaction (P < 0.05) between the type of fat and OE was observed in HSP70 liver expression (Fig. 2). Birds fed the diet with fresh oil and OE showed lower HSP70 gene expression compared to those fed with fresh oil and no OE. Contrary, HSP70 gene expression was higher in birds fed diet with peroxidized oil and OE compared to those fed the peroxidized oil and no OE.Table 6

sec.title: Growth performance
sec.p: The inclusion of oxidized lipids to the diet has been shown to decrease growth rate and increase oxidative damage in poultry (Bacou et al., 2021). Peroxidized fats might have a negative impact in broiler performance in young and adult birds. Young birds digest oxidized fats poorly affecting diet metabolizable energy and hence their growth (Leeson, 1999). Also, young birds experience high oxidative stress, and consuming peroxidized fats can intensify this stress by depleting both dietary and stored vitamin E. Conversely, prolonged consumption of peroxidized fats in adult birds lead to significant losses of fat-soluble vitamins reducing the animal’s antioxidant capacity, leading to poorer performance (Sheehy et al., 1994). Tavárez et al. (2011) reported that broilers fed oxidized soy oil with a PV of 7 mEq of /kg diet had significantly reduced final body weight, body weight gain, and feed efficiency. However, other authors have found no negative effects of oxidized oil or fat on broiler chicken production parameters. Upton et al. (2009) reported that increasing the dietary concentration of oxidized poultry fat with PV ranging from 0.3 to 6 mEq fat/kg diet or oxidized soybean oil from 1, 2 or 3 mEq oil/kg diet, had no impact on body weight or FCR in young broilers. The inconsistent effects of oxidized fats on broiler performance might be related to varying experimental conditions. A meta-analysis examining the effects of peroxidized lipids on growth performance concluded that differences in the fatty acid profiles of different lipid sources, the percentage at which lipids are included in diets, the degree of peroxidation, the techniques used to induce peroxidation, the imprecision in lipid peroxidation quantification, and insufficient replication between investigations could all contribute to this inconsistency (Hung et al., 2017). In the present study, PV in the feed averaged 3.75 vs. 23.0 mEq/kg for fresh and peroxidized diets, respectively. With such levels, we would expect to observe differences in growth. However, there is still a controversy regarding the critical threshold level of PV in the feed required to elicit a negative effect on poultry performance due to significant prediction errors caused by the mentioned factors (Hung et al., 2017). In addition, the lack of significant differences might also be attributed to the presence of synthetic antioxidants in the feeds, which play a crucial role in the control of lipid peroxidation, especially in foods containing oils and fats. The synthetic antioxidant BHT (Butyl hydroxytoluene) is effective in stabilizing animal fats and preventing the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids, ensuring the stability and quality of fat feeds (Bernal Gómez et al., 2003). In a study involving peroxide fats fed to broiler chickens, the incorporation of a feed with a PV of 4 mEq/kg was sufficient to reduce growth performance. However, the inclusion of ethoxyquin, a synthetic antioxidant, significantly reduced the negative effects of the peroxidized fat (Cabel et al., 1988). The question of whether to include synthetic antioxidants in the experimental test diets or not is a difficult decision when using peroxidized fats. In our study, we opted to include BHT to simulate a similar scenario to commercial feeds, allowing us to assess the potential antioxidant effects of phytogenic additives added on top, which could have reduced or mitigated the effects on performance, obtaining the results shown in this study. On the other hand, even though growth performance is the most important and reported measure, it may not be the most sensitive or consistent when utilizing oxidized lipids as a challenge model of oxidative distress in poultry (Bacou et al., 2021).

In the present study, broilers fed olive pomace extract showed a lower ADG from 1 to 10 days of age because of a reduced feed intake. This is in contrast with the findings of Corrales et al. (2023), who observed improved FCR in broilers after feeding a similar extract with comparable OE concentration during the first week of the trial. Xie et al. (2022) reported a significant decrease of ADFI feeding broilers with 0.4 and 0.5% of oleuropein, without affecting the FCR, in the first period of the trial (from 1 to 21 days). Also, Sulaiman et al. (2025) showed a lower BW from 7 to 10 days of age in birds supplemented with 125, 250 and 500 mg/kg of oleuropein, with a trend to recover these weight differences at the end of the trial. Oleuropein is a molecule with bitter taste (Ferlisi et al., 2023) and could be responsible for the less ADFI and BW in these trials, not affecting the FCR. Furthermore, the presence of peroxidized and subsequently rancid oil, in combination with the oleuropein, may explain the differences in ADFI observed in the present study during the first period (1 to 11 days) due to the reduced palatability of the feeds, also explaining possible discrepancies between trials. However, FCR during the first period was not affected in the present research. In the second period and over the entire trial period (1 to 21 days of age), no significant effects were observed on performance, in agreement with results obtained by Corrales et al. (2023) and Sevillano et al. (2025). In contrast, birds fed the spicy extract had better FCR from 1 to 10 days of age when the basal diet contained peroxidized oil. This is consistent with other studies in which broilers were subjected to stressful conditions, such as high density or poor hygienic conditions, and fed spices, including capsaicin (Thiamhirunsopit et al., 2014; Bravo et al., 2014; and Pirgozliev et al., 2014). However, this positive effect was not observed during the second period, and no significant effect was reported over the entire trial period (from 1 to 21 days of age).

sec.title: Antioxidant response and oxidative stress biomarkers
sec.p: The thermal processing of the soybean oil reflected a reduced vitamin E and increased hexanal concentrations in the peroxidized fat feeds, which agrees with Kerr et al. (2020). Since the concentration of vitamin E in the feed was lower, the levels of both alpha and gamma tocopherols in plasma were significantly lower in animals fed with oxidized fats. This effect was expected given the direct correlation between vitamin E intake and its plasma levels in poultry (Sklan et al., 1982; Hassan and Hakkarainen, 1990; Bölükbaşı et al., 2007). Supporting the results of the present study, a meta-analysis carried out by Hung et al. (2017) also indicates that feeding swine or poultry with peroxidized fat sources decreases the plasma or serum vitamin E levels. The alpha-tocopherol transfer protein is a cytosolic protein that plays an important role in regulating the α-tocopherol levels in the circulatory system (Koh et al., 2013) and it is encoded by TTPA gene. In the present study, we showed an upregulation of liver TTPA expression in birds fed fresh oil, compared to those fed the peroxidized oil. This might reflect the higher vitamin E concentrations in plasma in birds fed the fresh oil diets as previously indicated. However, Rengaraj et al. (2019) and Sevillano et al. (2025), did not found statistically significant upregulations in liver TTPA expression when increasing the vitamin E supplementation in broilers feeds (from 0 to 100 UI and to 100 ppm, respectively). The discrepancies between studies can be explained as vitamin E regulates the activity of liver TTPA in terms of protein stability and post-transcriptional levels, as Thakur et al. (2010) suggested. As Koh et al. (2013) demonstrated, liver TTPA expression is regulated by the liver X receptor (LXR), a nuclear receptor that directly interacts with the TTPA gene promoter, activating its expression and consequently increasing vitamin E levels in plasma. Therefore, peroxidized lipids and its derivative products could act as LXR agonists in a complex interplay, decreasing its activity. Thus, it is plausible that the lower TTPA expression in birds fed the oxidized oil might be through LXR signaling.

Scientific evidence in poultry suggests that feeding peroxidized fats induces oxidative stress (Bacou et al., 2021). Measuring oxidative stress requires assessing both oxidative damage and antioxidant defense systems. In the present study, plasma TBARS, a common lipid peroxidation biomarker, was not significantly affected by any of the factors (oil source, OE or SPICY). However, non-enzymatic antioxidant markers measured in plasma (FRAP and DPPH) showed increased values in birds fed peroxidized soybean oil compared to those fed fresh oil. The FRAP assay measures the reduction power of plasma, reflecting its antioxidant potential (Benzie and Strain, 1996). Thus, higher FRAP values implies greater antioxidant capacity, suggesting that the addition of peroxidized oil in the feed triggered an increase plasma antioxidant capacity. Similarly, DPPH assay measures the direct free radical scavenging potential (Mishra et al., 2012), so it can also indicate the antioxidant capacity of the plasma. In this study, DPPH values tended to be higher in birds fed peroxidized oil, aligning with the results of the FRAP assay. Moreover, broilers fed the peroxidized soybean oil increased the enzymatic antioxidant CAT activity and tended to increase that of GPx in plasma. All these findings partially agree with the study of Dong et al. (2020) who showed increased CAT activity, but higher TBARS concentrations and a decrease of the total antioxidant capacity in the serum of broilers fed peroxidized soybean oil. On the other hand, Liang et al. (2015) reported increments of plasma TBARS in broilers that fed peroxidized soybean oil, but with a significant CAT activity decrease. Lindblom et al. (2019) reported no significant effects on plasma TBARS, FRAP and CAT activity, but decreased GPx activity in broilers fed peroxidized soybean oil. The type and duration of the stress, the physiological state of the birds and the complex metabolic mechanisms and pathways behind the oxidant/antioxidant balance might explain discrepancies between studies and between the different biomarkers (Surai et al., 2019; Bacou et al., 2021). Therefore, in the present study, since no differences were found in TBARS values, the results appear to indicate that animals fed peroxidized fats successfully increased their non-enzymatic and enzymatic antioxidant response to counteract the effects of peroxidized fats and the reduced vitamin E levels in the feed.

In recent years, the benefits of plant-derived natural antioxidants in improving the antioxidant status of animals, and thus, enhancing performance and the quality and traits of animal products, have been extensively studied (Tsiplakou et al., 2021). In the present study, it was noteworthy that the interaction observed between OE and the type of fat, in such a way that in these OE-supplemented animals, the activity of the CAT enzyme in plasma did not increase with peroxidized fat, with a trend of GPx activity in the same direction. Given that no significant effects were observed on plasma TBARS among diets, this seems to indicate that animals fed with OE do not need to increase their antioxidant response to peroxidized fat, probably due to better control of oxidative processes. Gene expression analyses in the liver were in line with the observed in plasma as CAT gene expression was lower in birds fed the OE. This agrees with Galano et al. (2012) as HT has demonstrated to be a highly efficient free radical scavenger, which may reduce the free radicals and oxidative burden on the liver, causing a downregulation of CAT liver expression. Moreover, a significant interaction was observed between fat type and OE on HSP70. In birds fed fresh oil and OE the HSP70 expression was lower than in diets without OE, but it was upregulated in birds fed peroxidized oil and OE. Heat shock proteins are not highly expressed under normal physiological conditions, but they become increasingly active in response to several stressors, including oxidative stress, to repair and adjust to redox-related damages and alterations (Zhang et al., 2022). The use of antioxidants attenuates the activation of HSP70 by reducing the stress-causing agent. In this way, in heat stressed broilers, the use of plant extracts containing flavonoids, curcumin, or resveratrol, reduced the levels of HSP70 indicative of alleviated heat stress due to dietary supplementation (Shehata et al., 2020). But, at the same time, it has been documented that plant extracts or amino acids with antioxidant properties, such taurine and glutamine, can alleviate heat stress by enhancing antioxidant function and cell survival by increasing HSP70 expression (Shehata et al., 2020). Olive polyphenols could help to maintain the antioxidant balance of the birds by directly scavenging the free radicals or inducing antioxidant enzymes. Furthermore, HSP70 expression can be up- or down-regulated by the triterpenes in olive oil. They can accomplish that either directly by attaching themselves to the HSP70 gene nucleotide-binding domain or indirectly by blocking the transcription factor HSF1, which controls the expression of the gene (Yurasakpong et al., 2021). It is plausible that the effects observed in the present study indicated better control of the oxidative state in chickens fed with OE by activating HSP70 in the presence of peroxidized fats, which helps to maintain basal levels of CAT both in plasma and liver, rather than a more intense response as seen in diets without OE.

Despite no significant effects of SPICY were observed on plasma antioxidant response, CAT liver gene expression was affected by SPICY, being upregulated in birds fed this additive, with SOD showing a similar trend. Additionally, the HSP70 liver expression was downregulated in response to SPICY supplementation. These results agree with those reported by Liu et al. (2021), who showed an increment of CAT activity in liver broiler chickens fed 80 ppm of Capsicum extract (with GPx also showing increased values). Another compound in the spicy blend is the ginger extract, which has also been shown to increase SOD and CAT hepatic activity in broiler chickens (Al-Khalaifah et al., 2022). However, the study performed by Herrero-Encinas et al. (2023), in which broilers were fed 250 ppm of a similar spiced extract, showed contrary effects, as the extract downregulated the liver CAT and Nrf2 expression. According to these authors, the protective effects of phytogenics in intestine could downregulate antioxidant enzyme expression in peripheral organs, making upregulation unnecessary in the liver. Finally, Sancho et al. (2003) reported that CAT activity can suppress the 70- or 27-kDa heat-shock protein expression and the inhibition of heat-shock transcription factor 1 binding activity, which could explain the downregulation of the liver HPS70 in birds fed the SPICY. Given that the antioxidant responses observed in this study are limited to the starter phase, assessing the influence of these additives across the complete growth cycle warrants future investigation.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Under our experimental conditions, the inclusion of peroxidized soybean oil in the feed of broilers did not affect the productive parameters from 1 to 21 days of age. However, the presence of lipid peroxidation products in the feed triggered both non-enzymatic and enzymatic antioxidant responses to maintain the oxidant/antioxidant balance. In the case of birds fed the olive pomace extract, the enzymatic antioxidant response was more attenuated, indicating a better control of oxidative stress, likely mediated by HSP70. Our results suggest that phytogenic additives may help sustain antioxidant balance even when performance improvements are limited under practical feed fat oxidation conditions.
